newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Dresdner chases profits in phone bank market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dresdner chases profits in phone bank market.

text.p: Dresdner Bank AG on Wednesday said its soon-to-be launched direct banking unit would stand out from the crowd by offering a more comprehensive service than its rivals and generating strong profits.

Dresdner plans to start the phone-based unit in the second half of 1997, becoming the last of Germany's Big Five banks to fully target the market for branchless banking, which is expected to mushroom dramatically in the coming years.

Board member Heinz-Joerg Platzek said Dresdner used its extra planning time to develop a unit which would break even in five years and yield an average 15 percent net return on its starting capital of 150 million marks ($99.60 million) in the first 10 years.
"You will see, we are building a completely new type of bank," Platzek told a news conference.
Dresdner is counting on attracting at least 500,000 customers to the new unit, which has yet to be named, within the next ten years.
"This will be highly profitable ... Our return projections are based on a worst-case scenario," Platzek said.

While he declined to detail the full cost of the unit, or reveal its opening hours or products, Platzek said the direct bank's product range would be as broad as that of a regular bank -- unlike less comprehensive services on offer elsewhere.
There was a huge and heterogeneous potential market for direct banking services, in Germany and Europe as a whole, which had not yet been accurately identified or tapped.
"The potential customers for direct banking come from every client group now in the branch network," he said.

While 95 percent of Germans today rely on conventional banking relationships based around the local branch, only 20 percent of customers would still be satisfied with these traditional services by the year 2010, Platzek predicted.

Today, some 220,000 of Dresdner's six million retail clients are using telephone or PC banking as well as their branch but 50 to 60 percent of customers were expected to operate in this way by 2010 and up to 30 percent would opt solely for a direct bank.

Dresdner said it would employ fully trained bank employees at its new unit, not the students and housewives on which many direct banks rely, and would thus be able to offer full advisory services. The unit will have 170 staff at the start.

"We don't want to be a cheap bank," Platzek said, adding that while the direct service would still be considerably cheaper than conventional banking services, it would also cater for the profitable segment of upscale clients.

Deutsche Bank AG, Commerzbank AG Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG have all set up telephone banking units in a bid to woo customers and make their cost-laden retail banking businesses more efficient.
Deutsche has attracted 60,000 accounts to its year-old Bank 24 unit and is aiming at 500,000 by the year 2,000.
Until now, Dresdner lagged behind, saying it wanted to wait until the market was more mature, after abandoning an early direct banking project developed six years ago.
Platzek said Dresdner's ambitions in direct banking were not restricted to Germany and that the launch of the Euro would create new oppportunities throughout Europe.
"We believe that the Euro will come in January 1999 and this direct bank will be ideally suited to target the European direct banking market," he said.
